title: Single-Cell RNA-seq and TCR-seq for Immunologists
text:
Welcome
This is a six-week, hands-on course for graduate students in immunology who want to analyse single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) and paired single-cell TCR-seq (scTCR-seq) data with confidence. It assumes you understand immunology well and programming a little. Every analysis step is taught twice: conceptually (what the algorithm does and why) and practically, in both R / Seurat and Python / Scanpy. Pick one language and stick with it, or read both to see how the ideas transfer.

title: Single-Cell RNA-seq and TCR-seq for Immunologists
text:
How the course is organised
Each weekly session is one chapter and runs about 2.5 hours: roughly 45 minutes of concept discussion followed by 90 minutes of guided coding. Every chapter follows the same template:

Learning objectives
Concepts — the ideas behind the step, with diagrams and immunology-specific commentary
Hands-on — code shown in an R tab and a Python tab
Pitfalls — the mistakes we see most often
Exercises — to complete before the next session




Week
Chapter
Core question




1
From cells to counts
What is actually in a count matrix, and which barcodes are real cells?


2
Normalization and PCA
How do we make cells comparable and compress 20,000 genes into a useful space?


3
Neighbours, clustering, UMAP
How do we find groups of similar cells, and how should we (not) read a UMAP?


4
Annotation
Which immune cell types and states are these clusters?


5
TCR repertoire
What are the clonotypes, how expanded are they, and which phenotypes do they occupy?


6
Multi-sample analysis and capstone
How do we compare conditions honestly, and track clones across samples?

title: Single-Cell RNA-seq and TCR-seq for Immunologists
text:
The dataset
We use a single public 10x Genomics dataset throughout: human PBMCs profiled with the Chromium 5′ Immune Profiling workflow, which yields a gene expression library and a paired TCR V(D)J library from the same cells. One dataset carried across all six weeks means you build one complete analysis rather than six disconnected snippets. The Setup appendix explains how to download it.






TipWorking with your own data



Everything here transfers directly to tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes, sorted T cell populations, mouse samples or multi-timepoint studies. Where mouse-specific changes are needed (gene symbols, mitochondrial gene prefix, reference atlases) we say so.

title: 1  From Cells to Counts
text: 1.1 Concepts

title: 1  From Cells to Counts
text:
1.1.1 What the 10x Chromium actually measures
A droplet-based scRNA-seq experiment does three things: it isolates single cells in droplets, tags every mRNA molecule in a droplet with a cell barcode (shared by all molecules from that droplet) and a unique molecular identifier, UMI (unique to each captured molecule), and then converts those tagged molecules into a sequencing library.







 The 10x workflow. The same barcoded cDNA feeds both the gene expression (GEX) and the V(D)J library, which is what lets us pair a TCR sequence to a transcriptome. 





1.1.2 How a transcript gets its barcode: 3′ chemistry
Inside each droplet there is one gel bead carrying millions of copies of a single oligonucleotide. Every copy has the same cell barcode (so everything in the droplet gets the same label) and a different UMI (so each captured molecule gets its own tag). The oligo’s job is to attach itself to a cDNA copy of every mRNA in the droplet. How it does that differs between the two chemistries, and the difference is where the barcode ends up on the molecule.






Figure 1.1: The 3′ workflow. The bead oligo ends in poly(dT), which captures the mRNA by its poly(A) tail. Reverse transcription then copies the mRNA from its 3′ end toward its 5′ end; a template-switch oligo (TSO) free in solution caps the far end. The barcode is therefore next to the transcript’s 3′ end.




Reading Figure 1.1, step by step. The bead oligo is, from the bead outward: a sequencing-primer site (Read 1), the cell barcode, the UMI, and a stretch of ~30 T’s, poly(dT). mRNAs end in a poly(A) tail, so poly(dT) base-pairs with it (step 1). Reverse transcriptase (RT) then extends from the poly(dT), synthesising cDNA along the mRNA toward its 5′ end (step 2). When RT reaches the 5′ cap it adds a few untemplated cytosines, and a template-switch oligo (TSO) in the reaction mix, ending in three riboguanosines (rGrGrG), anneals to them; RT “switches template” and copies the TSO, so the cDNA ends with a known sequence that later serves as a PCR handle (step 3).
The result is a single molecule: Read 1 → barcode → UMI → poly(dT) → the transcript copied from its 3′ end to its 5′ end → TSO. Because sequencing starts from Read 1, the ~100 nt of transcript that actually get sequenced are the ones next to poly(dT): the 3′ end of the gene.



1.1.3 5′ chemistry: the same parts, rearranged






Figure 1.2: The 5′ workflow. The poly(dT) primer is now free in solution and the TSO is on the bead. First-strand cDNA is made without the bead’s involvement; only when RT reaches the 5′ cap and adds CCC does the cDNA dock onto the bead’s rGrGrG, and RT then copies barcode and UMI into it. The barcode is therefore next to the transcript’s 5′ end.




Reading Figure 1.2. Nothing chemically new happens; the two oligos have swapped places. Poly(dT) is now a free primer, so RT still starts at the poly(A) tail and copies toward the 5′ end, adding CCC when it runs off the cap (step 1). But the rGrGrG that captures those C’s is now on the bead oligo, so the cDNA docks onto the bead by its 5′-end-derived end (step 2). RT extends across the bead’s TSO, barcode and UMI, copying them into the cDNA (step 3).
The result is Read 1 → barcode → UMI → TSO → the transcript from its 5′ end to its 3′ end → poly(dT). Sequencing from Read 1 now reads the 5′ end of the gene. For ordinary gene counting this makes little difference: a 5′ read maps to a gene about as well as a 3′ read. For TCRs it makes all the difference.



1.1.4 From one cDNA pool to two libraries
After reverse transcription the droplets are broken and every cell’s barcoded cDNA is amplified together in one tube. That pool is then split. One aliquot is fragmented and sequenced as the gene expression (GEX) library. Another is put through a targeted PCR to make the V(D)J library. Both libraries descend from the same molecules, which is why a TCR and a transcriptome with the same barcode came from the same cell.






Figure 1.3: Top: the 5′ barcoded cDNA of a TCR transcript and the two libraries made from it. The GEX library reads a random ~90 nt of transcript beside the barcode; the V(D)J library amplifies from the Read 1 site to a primer at the start of the constant region, capturing leader, V, CDR3 and J. Bottom: the same V(D)J PCR on a 3′ cDNA. The constant-region primer now sits between the barcode and the CDR3, so the amplicon stops before it.




Why 3′ chemistry cannot give you a CDR3 (Figure 1.3). A TCR mRNA runs 5′ → leader → V → (D) → J → C → 3′ UTR → poly(A). The CDR3 is the V–(D)–J junction. The V(D)J library is made by PCR between a forward primer on the Read 1 site (at the barcode end) and reverse primers that sit at the very start of the constant region, just downstream of J. PCR copies only what lies between two primers.

On 5′ cDNA the barcode sits beside the leader, so the region between the primers is leader → V → CDR3 → J → the first few bases of C. Every amplicon contains a complete CDR3, and it is still attached to the barcode and UMI. After fragmentation and sequencing, Cell Ranger collects all reads sharing a barcode and UMI, assembles them into a full-length contig, and calls the V gene, J gene and CDR3 from it.
On 3′ cDNA the barcode sits beside the 3′ UTR. The same constant-region primer now points back toward the barcode across the 3′ UTR, and the amplicon is 3′ UTR → C. The CDR3 lies on the far side of the primer, outside every amplicon. You can detect that the cell expresses TRBC1; you can never read which V, J and CDR3 it used. Moving the primer does not help, because any primer placed upstream of the CDR3 would be pointing away from the barcode.

The rule that follows: paired TCR (or BCR) and transcriptome data require the 5′ chemistry. If you are handed a 3′ dataset, repertoire analysis is not an option.







Note



The 5′ kit reads the 5′ end of every transcript, not just TCRs, so its gene-expression data look slightly different from 3′ data: genes with long 5′ UTRs or alternative first exons behave differently, and mitochondrial genes are detected at lower fractions. Do not compare 3′ and 5′ datasets without integration (Week 6).




1.1.5 The count matrix
After alignment and UMI collapsing, Cell Ranger produces a matrix with one row per gene and one column per cell barcode. Values are integer UMI counts, i.e. the number of distinct mRNA molecules detected per gene per cell. Two properties of this matrix drive every downstream decision:

It is sparse. A typical T cell has ~1,000–3,000 detected genes out of ~36,000 in the annotation. Roughly 90–95% of entries are zero. Most zeros are not “the gene is off”; they are sampling failure, because a 10x experiment captures perhaps 10–20% of a cell’s mRNA. This is why we normalize, why we pool information across cells, and why a single zero means little.
Library size varies enormously. One cell may yield 800 UMIs and its neighbour 12,000, for reasons that have nothing to do with biology (droplet-to-droplet capture efficiency, cell size, RNA content). We will address this in Week 2.


What is a “cell” to Cell Ranger? Nothing biological. Every droplet gets a barcode, including the vast majority that contain no cell and only ambient RNA from lysed cells in the suspension. Cell Ranger’s cell-calling step (EmptyDrops-based) separates barcodes whose expression profile differs from the ambient background from those that look like empty droplets. The filtered matrix contains the called cells; the raw matrix contains every barcode. You almost always start from the filtered matrix, but the raw matrix is needed for ambient-RNA correction tools (SoupX, CellBender).



1.1.6 Quality control metrics
Three per-cell metrics catch most problems:









Metric
What it measures
Low values suggest
High values suggest




nCount / total_counts
Total UMIs in the barcode
Empty droplet, dying cell, or a small quiescent cell
Doublet, or a large/active cell


nFeature / n_genes
Number of genes with ≥1 UMI
Same as above
Same as above


percent.mt / pct_counts_mt
Fraction of UMIs from mitochondrial genes
—
Cytoplasmic mRNA leaked from a damaged membrane while mitochondria stayed put




Immune-specific QC considerations

Naive and resting lymphocytes are small and RNA-poor. They sit at the low end of the UMI distribution legitimately. Aggressive minimum-UMI thresholds selectively remove naive T and B cells, biasing your composition.
Activated T cells, plasmablasts and cycling cells are RNA-rich and have high mitochondrial content because of oxidative metabolism. A fixed 5% mitochondrial cutoff, borrowed from other tissues, will delete real effector biology. Look at the distribution per cluster before deciding, and consider 10–15% for PBMCs, higher for tissue-derived or stimulated cells.
Platelets and red blood cells appear as clusters with PPBP/PF4 or HBB/HBA1. They are not doublets or low-quality cells, just contaminants of a PBMC prep. Remove them explicitly after clustering, not with QC thresholds.
Ambient TCR transcripts. Because TCR mRNAs are abundant and lymphocytes lyse readily, TRBC1/TRAC counts appear in monocytes. This is ambient contamination, not myeloid cells expressing a TCR.




1.1.7 Doublets
At standard 10x loading (~5–10k cells recovered), 4–8% of “cells” are two cells that shared a droplet. Heterotypic doublets (a T cell plus a monocyte) form spurious intermediate clusters and are the classic source of “novel” cell types in reviews. Homotypic doublets (two CD4 T cells) are nearly undetectable by expression and mostly harmless for clustering, but they matter for TCR-seq because a doublet has two α and two β chains, which looks like a rare dual-TCR cell.
Doublet detectors (scDblFinder, Scrublet, DoubletFinder) all work the same way: they create synthetic doublets by adding pairs of real cells together, then flag real cells that look more like the synthetic doublets than like other real cells. Run them per 10x lane, never on a merged object, because doublets can only form within a lane.

We assume you have completed the Setup appendix and have filtered_feature_bc_matrix.h5 in data/raw/.

1.2.1 Load the count matrix

library(Seurat)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

counts <- Read10X_h5("data/raw/filtered_feature_bc_matrix.h5")

# 5' Immune Profiling runs may return a list if antibody capture was included
if (is.list(counts)) counts <- counts[["Gene Expression"]]

dim(counts)              # genes x cells
counts[1:5, 1:5]         # a sparse dgCMatrix: "." means zero
mean(counts == 0)        # fraction of zeros, typically > 0.9

pbmc <- CreateSeuratObject(
  counts       = counts,
  project      = "pbmc_5p",
  min.cells    = 3,       # drop genes seen in < 3 cells
  min.features = 200      # drop barcodes with < 200 genes (very permissive)
)
pbmc


import scanpy as sc
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

sc.settings.verbosity = 2
sc.settings.set_figure_params(dpi=100, facecolor="white")

adata = sc.read_10x_h5("data/raw/filtered_feature_bc_matrix.h5")
adata.var_names_make_unique()

adata                     # AnnData: obs = cells, var = genes, X = counts
adata.X[:5, :5].toarray()
1 - adata.X.nnz / np.prod(adata.shape)   # fraction of zeros

# Very permissive first pass; real thresholds come after inspection
sc.pp.filter_cells(adata, min_genes=200)
sc.pp.filter_genes(adata, min_cells=3)
adata









Note



Scanpy stores cells as rows and genes as columns (cells × genes); Seurat stores genes as rows and cells as columns (genes × cells). This is the most common source of confusion when reading both.




1.2.2 Compute QC metrics

R (Seurat)Python (Scanpy)


# Human mitochondrial genes start with "MT-"; mouse uses "mt-"
pbmc[["percent.mt"]]   <- PercentageFeatureSet(pbmc, pattern = "^MT-")
pbmc[["percent.ribo"]] <- PercentageFeatureSet(pbmc, pattern = "^RP[SL]")
pbmc[["percent.hb"]]   <- PercentageFeatureSet(pbmc, pattern = "^HB[AB]")

VlnPlot(pbmc,
        features = c("nFeature_RNA", "nCount_RNA", "percent.mt"),
        ncol = 3, pt.size = 0)

# Relationships between metrics are more informative than any one alone
FeatureScatter(pbmc, "nCount_RNA", "percent.mt") +
FeatureScatter(pbmc, "nCount_RNA", "nFeature_RNA")

# Log scale reveals the low-UMI tail where empty droplets and debris hide
ggplot(pbmc@meta.data, aes(nCount_RNA, nFeature_RNA, colour = percent.mt)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.3) + scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  scale_colour_viridis_c()


adata.var["mt"]   = adata.var_names.str.startswith("MT-")   # "mt-" for mouse
adata.var["ribo"] = adata.var_names.str.startswith(("RPS", "RPL"))
adata.var["hb"]   = adata.var_names.str.contains("^HB[AB]")

sc.pp.calculate_qc_metrics(
    adata, qc_vars=["mt", "ribo", "hb"],
    percent_top=[20], log1p=True, inplace=True
)

sc.pl.violin(
    adata, ["n_genes_by_counts", "total_counts", "pct_counts_mt"],
    jitter=0.4, multi_panel=True
)
sc.pl.scatter(adata, x="total_counts", y="pct_counts_mt")
sc.pl.scatter(adata, x="total_counts", y="n_genes_by_counts", color="pct_counts_mt")

# scDblFinder (Bioconductor) is fast and well-calibrated
library(scDblFinder)
library(SingleCellExperiment)

sce <- as.SingleCellExperiment(pbmc)
set.seed(1)
sce <- scDblFinder(sce)      # add samples = "lane" if you have several lanes
pbmc$doublet_score <- sce$scDblFinder.score
pbmc$doublet_class <- sce$scDblFinder.class
table(pbmc$doublet_class)


# Scrublet is built into scanpy >= 1.10
sc.pp.scrublet(adata, random_state=0)   # add batch_key="lane" for several lanes
adata.obs["predicted_doublet"].value_counts()
sc.pl.scrublet_score_distribution(adata)

Choose thresholds from your distributions, not from a tutorial. The values below suit a healthy-donor PBMC run; write down what you chose and why.

pbmc <- subset(pbmc,
  nFeature_RNA > 300 &
  nFeature_RNA < 5000 &
  percent.mt  < 12 &
  doublet_class == "singlet"
)
pbmc

saveRDS(pbmc, "data/processed/01_pbmc_qc.rds")


keep = (
    (adata.obs["n_genes_by_counts"] > 300) &
    (adata.obs["n_genes_by_counts"] < 5000) &
    (adata.obs["pct_counts_mt"] < 12) &
    (~adata.obs["predicted_doublet"].astype(bool))
)

adata.write_h5ad("data/processed/01_pbmc_qc.h5ad")

title: 1  From Cells to Counts
text:
1.3 Pitfalls


Filtering on a hard upper UMI cutoff to remove doublets. It removes plasmablasts, proliferating T cells and monocytes preferentially. Use a doublet detector instead and keep the upper bound generous.
Using a 5% mitochondrial cutoff because a tutorial did. Set it from the distribution and re-examine per cluster in Week 3.
Running doublet detection on merged lanes. Doublets cannot form across lanes; merging inflates the synthetic-doublet space with impossible pairs.
Forgetting the raw matrix exists. If you later want SoupX or CellBender, you need raw_feature_bc_matrix; download it now.
Treating zeros as evidence of absence. A T cell with zero CD4 UMIs is usually a CD4 T cell that was under-sampled. This is why we never annotate single cells from single genes.

text:
1.4 Exercises

Plot percent.mt against nCount_RNA on a log-x axis. Describe the two or three populations you see and propose a biological identity for each.
Re-run the filter with mitochondrial thresholds of 5%, 10% and 20%. How many cells does each remove? In Week 3 you will check which clusters lost cells.
Cell Ranger reported a certain number of cells. How many does your filtered object contain? Where did the difference go?
(Stretch) Load the raw matrix and plot the barcode-rank (“knee”) plot: total UMIs per barcode, sorted, on log–log axes. Mark where Cell Ranger placed its cell-calling threshold.

title: 2  Normalization and Principal Components
text: 2.1 Concepts

title: 2  Normalization and Principal Components
text:
2.1.1 Normalization: making cells comparable
Two cells with identical biology can differ tenfold in total UMIs purely through capture efficiency. Before we can say “cell A expresses more GZMB than cell B” we must remove that global scaling factor.
The standard approach has two steps:

Library-size scaling. Divide each cell’s counts by its total UMIs and multiply by a common target (10,000 is conventional), giving counts-per-10k (CP10k). Every cell now “has” 10,000 UMIs.
Log transform. Take \(\log(x + 1)\). This compresses the dynamic range so that a highly expressed gene like B2M (thousands of counts) does not dominate every distance computation, stabilises the variance, and makes differences roughly proportional (a doubling is the same distance everywhere).







Figure 2.1: Two cells with identical composition but a fourfold difference in capture. Dividing by library size makes them comparable; the log then shrinks the gap between abundant and rare genes so that no single gene dominates the distances computed later.




Why the +1? \(\log(0)\) is undefined, and most entries are zero. The pseudocount keeps zeros at zero. It has a known side effect: for lowly expressed genes it creates a spurious relationship between library size and normalized value, which is one motivation for SCTransform.

SCTransform (Hafemeister & Satija, 2019) takes a different route. It fits a regularised negative-binomial regression of each gene’s counts on sequencing depth, then uses the Pearson residuals (how far each observed count deviates from what the model predicts for a cell of that depth) as the normalized value. Residuals are centred, variance-stabilised and free of the depth artefact. In practice both methods yield similar clusters on PBMCs; SCTransform tends to separate subtle states a little better and log-normalization is simpler to interpret. We show log-normalization as the default and note SCTransform in the code.


2.1.2 Feature selection: highly variable genes
Of ~20,000 detected genes, most vary between cells only through sampling noise (housekeeping genes) or are so rare they carry no signal. Including them in distance computations adds noise. We therefore pick ~2,000 highly variable genes (HVGs): genes whose variance across cells exceeds what we expect from their mean expression alone.
The key insight is that in count data variance rises with the mean, so “most variable” naively just means “most highly expressed”. HVG methods fit the mean–variance trend and select genes that sit above it. The vst / seurat_v3 method does this on raw counts; the older dispersion method does it on log-normalized data after binning by mean.

Immune data and HVGs. Cell-type marker genes (CD3E, MS4A1, LYZ) reliably become HVGs because they are on in some cells and off in others. So do TCR and immunoglobulin variable genes (TRBV*, IGKV*), for the wrong reason: each clone uses a different V gene, so these genes vary enormously between cells without reflecting cell state. If your T cell clusters split by clone rather than by phenotype, exclude TRAV/TRBV/TRDV/TRGV/IGHV/IGKV/IGLV genes from the HVG list. We show how below.



2.1.3 Scaling
Even after log-normalization, genes live on very different scales. B2M sits around 6–7 log units in every cell and wobbles by a unit or two through sampling noise. FOXP3 is zero in most cells and around 0.5–1 in Tregs. That on/off pattern is the biology we care about, but in raw log units B2M’s noise is several times larger than FOXP3’s signal. Any method that measures distance between cells would be listening to B2M.






Figure 2.2: Before scaling (left) the spread of an abundant gene dwarfs the spread of a rare but informative one. After z-scoring (right) each gene has mean 0 and standard deviation 1, so a Treg’s FOXP3 now counts as much as any other gene’s variation.



Scaling fixes this by z-scoring each HVG across cells: subtract the gene’s mean, divide by its standard deviation. Every gene now has mean 0 and unit variance, so each contributes equally to what follows. The cost is that a gene’s absolute expression level is thrown away; only relative patterns across cells remain, which is exactly what we want for finding structure. Values are usually clipped (e.g. at ±10) so that a single extreme cell cannot define a principal component on its own.


2.1.4 Principal component analysis
We now have a matrix of ~10,000 cells in a ~2,000-dimensional gene space. Distances in 2,000 dimensions are noisy (every gene contributes sampling error) and expensive. PCA finds a much smaller set of axes that capture most of the structured variation.
Start with just two genes so the picture fits on a page.






Figure 2.3: Left: cells plotted by scaled CD3E and LYZ. The cloud is a diagonal streak because the two genes are anti-correlated. PC1 is the direction of that streak; PC2 is perpendicular to it. Middle: the same cells with the axes rotated so PC1 is horizontal; nearly all the spread is now along one axis. Right: an elbow plot from real PBMC data.




PCA, geometrically. In Figure 2.3 (A) every cell is a point whose coordinates are its scaled CD3E and LYZ values. Monocytes sit top-left (high LYZ, low CD3E); T cells sit bottom-right. The cloud is not round; it is a streak. PCA asks one question: along which single direction do the points spread out the most? That direction is PC1, drawn as the long arrow. It then asks the same question restricted to directions perpendicular to PC1, giving PC2, and so on for as many dimensions as there are genes.
Panel (B) rotates the picture so PC1 lies flat. Each cell’s position along that axis is its PC1 score. Notice that the PC2 scores are all close to zero: almost none of the variation was lost by dropping PC2. We compressed two genes into one number without losing the monocyte-versus-T-cell information.
A worked example. Take the five labelled cells. After scaling their (CD3E, LYZ) values are A = (−1.2, 1.1), B = (−0.9, 0.8), C = (0.9, −1.0), D = (1.1, −0.9), E = (0.1, 0.0). PC1 points along (0.71, −0.71): that is, it is the weighted sum \(0.71 \times \text{CD3E} - 0.71 \times \text{LYZ}\). Those weights are the loadings. A cell’s PC1 score is just that sum: A scores \(0.71(-1.2) - 0.71(1.1) = -1.6\), C scores \(+1.3\), E scores \(+0.07\). PC2 uses loadings (0.71, 0.71); A scores \(-0.07\), C scores \(-0.07\). Every cell has a large PC1 score and a tiny PC2 score, which is the numerical version of “the streak is one-dimensional”.
In real data there are 2,000 HVGs instead of two, so each PC is a weighted sum of 2,000 genes and there are 2,000 possible PCs. The geometry is identical; we just cannot draw it. Mathematically the PCs are the eigenvectors of the gene–gene covariance matrix and the variance along each PC is the corresponding eigenvalue, which is what the elbow plot in panel (C) shows.








 Why we reduce dimensions: genes co-vary in programmes, so a few axes summarise thousands of genes. 



Two practical questions follow.
How many PCs? The elbow plot shows variance explained per PC. Typically the first 10–20 PCs each explain substantial variance and then the curve flattens into a floor of noise. Choosing anywhere from the elbow to slightly past it (commonly 20–40 PCs) is fine; downstream results are robust to this choice within reason. Too few PCs loses rare populations (which often live on a single mid-ranked PC); too many adds noise but rarely breaks anything.
What is each PC? Look at the loadings, as in Figure 2.4. PC1 in PBMCs is almost always lymphoid versus myeloid (LYZ, S100A8 on one side; CD3E, IL7R on the other). PC2 is often T/NK versus B. If a PC is loaded with ribosomal genes, MALAT1, mitochondrial genes, heat-shock genes or MKI67/TOP2A, that PC is tracking cell quality, dissociation stress or cell cycle rather than identity, and you should decide whether to regress that signal out.






Figure 2.4: Loadings for two PCs from a PBMC run. PC1 is interpretable biology. PC9 pits mitochondrial and stress transcripts against ribosomal ones: a quality axis that will pull dying cells into their own cluster if left alone.

2.2 Hands-on

2.2.1 Normalize

R (Seurat)Python (Scanpy)


library(Seurat)
pbmc <- readRDS("data/processed/01_pbmc_qc.rds")

# Default: log(CP10k + 1), stored in the "data" layer
pbmc <- NormalizeData(pbmc, normalization.method = "LogNormalize", scale.factor = 1e4)

# Alternative: SCTransform (creates an "SCT" assay; skip ScaleData if you use this)
# pbmc <- SCTransform(pbmc, vst.flavor = "v2", verbose = FALSE)

# Compare raw and normalized for one gene
LayerData(pbmc, layer = "counts")["CD3E", 1:5]
LayerData(pbmc, layer = "data")["CD3E", 1:5]


import scanpy as sc
adata = sc.read_h5ad("data/processed/01_pbmc_qc.h5ad")

# Keep raw counts: HVG selection (seurat_v3) and TCR/pseudobulk steps need them
adata.layers["counts"] = adata.X.copy()

sc.pp.normalize_total(adata, target_sum=1e4)
sc.pp.log1p(adata)

# Alternative: analytic Pearson residuals (SCTransform-like)
# sc.experimental.pp.normalize_pearson_residuals(adata)

text:
2.3 Pitfalls


Running PCA on unscaled data. A handful of abundant genes will define every PC.
Using all genes instead of HVGs. Slower and noisier, with no gain.
Leaving TCR/BCR V genes in the HVG set. Clones cluster separately, and clonal expansion masquerades as cell state.
Regressing out variables reflexively. Regressing out mitochondrial fraction or cell cycle removes real biology if those correlate with cell state (they do, for activated T cells). Inspect first, regress only if a PC is clearly technical.
Treating the number of PCs as sacred. Anything from 20 to 50 usually works. If you want to be careful, run downstream clustering with 20 and 40 PCs and check what changes.
Interpreting PC scores directly as cell types. PCs are axes of variance, not categories. PC1 separating lymphoid from myeloid does not mean “PC1 = monocyte score”.

title: 3  Neighbours, Clustering and UMAP
text: 3.1 Concepts

title: 3  Neighbours, Clustering and UMAP
text:
3.1.1 From points to a graph: k-nearest neighbours
After PCA each cell is a point in ~30-dimensional space. The next step builds a k-nearest-neighbour (kNN) graph: for each cell, find the \(k\) cells closest to it (Euclidean distance in PC space; \(k\) = 15–30 is typical) and draw an edge to each. The graph now encodes local structure: which cells are transcriptionally similar to which.
Seurat and Scanpy then refine this into a shared-nearest-neighbour (SNN) graph. Two cells are connected with weight proportional to how many neighbours they share (the Jaccard index of their neighbour sets). Two cells that are each other’s neighbours and have largely overlapping neighbourhoods are strongly connected; two cells that happen to be close but sit in different neighbourhoods are weakly connected. This makes the graph robust to a few cells lying between populations.






Figure 3.1: Building the graph. (A) Each cell is joined to its k closest cells in PC space. (B) Edges are re-weighted by how many neighbours the two cells share, so cells embedded in the same neighbourhood are tightly bound and cells that are merely nearby are weakly bound. (C) Community detection cuts the graph where edges are sparse.




Why a graph? In high dimensions, absolute distances are unreliable (the “curse of dimensionality”): almost everything is roughly equally far from everything else. Relative distance is reliable: “these are my 20 closest cells” is a stable statement even when “this cell is 3.7 units away” is not. Graph methods use only the relative information. Every downstream step in this chapter (clustering, UMAP, later trajectory inference) is a computation on this graph.








 The graph is the central object. Clustering and UMAP are two independent views of it. 





3.1.2 Clustering: community detection
Louvain and its successor Leiden are algorithms that partition a graph into communities: groups of nodes densely connected to each other and sparsely connected to the rest. They maximise modularity, a score that compares the number of edges inside communities with the number expected if edges were placed at random.
The resolution parameter scales how many edges “random” expects. Higher resolution means the algorithm is rewarded for finding smaller, tighter communities; lower resolution merges them. There is no correct resolution. Resolution 0.3 on PBMCs gives you T, B, NK, monocyte, DC; resolution 1.5 splits T cells into naive CD4, memory CD4, Treg, naive CD8, effector CD8, MAIT, γδ and a few clusters you will struggle to name. Both are valid descriptions at different granularities (Figure 3.2).






Figure 3.2: The same cells and the same graph, partitioned at two resolutions. Nothing about the data changed between the panels.




Clusters are hypotheses, not discoveries. The algorithm will always return clusters, including on data with no structure. A cluster is the statement “these cells are more similar to each other than to their neighbours at this resolution”. Whether that similarity corresponds to a cell type, a cell state, an activation gradient cut arbitrarily into pieces, a batch, or a quality artefact is a biological question answered in Week 4. Leiden is preferred over Louvain because it guarantees connected communities and is faster; results are otherwise similar.



3.1.3 UMAP: seeing the graph
Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection takes the same kNN graph and finds a 2-D layout in which cells that are neighbours in the graph end up close together. Roughly: it converts neighbour distances into edge probabilities (a fuzzy graph), then moves points around in 2-D so that connected cells attract and unconnected cells repel, minimising a cross-entropy between the high-dimensional and low-dimensional graphs.
Two parameters matter:

n_neighbors (default 15–30): the size of the neighbourhood UMAP tries to preserve. Small values emphasise fine local structure and fragment the plot; large values emphasise global arrangement and blur small populations.
min_dist (default 0.3–0.5): how tightly points may pack. Small values give dense, well-separated islands; large values give a diffuse cloud that better shows continua.







Figure 3.3: A schematic of what UMAP preserves. Left: the arrangement of populations in PC space. Right: the UMAP layout of the same cells. Neighbourhoods and the continuum survive; the distances between islands, their relative sizes and their shapes do not.




What a UMAP does and does not tell you (see Figure 3.3)
Reliable:

Cells in the same island are neighbours in the graph (local structure is preserved).
A continuous smear usually reflects a real gradient (e.g. naive → memory → effector).

Not reliable:

Distance between islands. UMAP places islands wherever the layout optimiser puts them. B cells being “far from” monocytes carries no quantitative meaning.
Island size. UMAP expands dense regions and compresses sparse ones. A big island is not a more heterogeneous population.
Shape. Arms, branches and rings are often artefacts of min_dist and random seed.
Anything you did not test in the graph or the expression matrix. UMAP is a picture of an analysis. It is not the analysis.

The clustering did not use the UMAP, and the UMAP did not use the clustering. When a cluster straddles two islands or an island contains two clusters, that is the graph and the layout disagreeing about ambiguous cells, not an error.

t-SNE is the older alternative. It preserves local structure similarly but has no meaningful global arrangement at all, is slower, and cannot embed new cells into an existing layout. UMAP has largely replaced it; the caveats above apply to both.


3.1.4 Assessing robustness
Because resolution is arbitrary and Leiden has a random component, check that clusters you intend to interpret survive perturbation:

Cluster at several resolutions and draw a cluster tree (clustree) to see which splits are stable across resolutions and which flicker.
Compute a silhouette score per cluster in PC space: cells with negative silhouette are closer to another cluster than their own.
Re-run with a different random seed and compare with the adjusted Rand index.
Check that no cluster is defined by nCount, percent.mt or cell-cycle phase alone.

title: 3  Neighbours, Clustering and UMAP
text:
3.3 Pitfalls


Clustering on the UMAP coordinates. Some tools let you. Never do it: UMAP has thrown away most of the information.
Reading distances between islands. “Tregs are closer to naive CD4 than to Th17 on the UMAP” is not a finding.
Reporting one resolution as the clustering. State the resolution, show the tree, and justify the granularity by the question.
Over-clustering then annotating every cluster as a distinct type. At resolution 2 a continuous activation gradient becomes six “subsets”.
Not checking QC per cluster. A cluster with low UMIs and high mitochondrial fraction is dying cells, not a novel population.
Forgetting the random seed. UMAP layouts and Leiden partitions are stochastic. Fix seeds for reproducibility; vary them to test robustness.

title: 4  Annotation: From Clusters to Immune Cell States
text:
4.1.1 Type versus state
A cell type is a stable lineage identity (CD4 T cell, monocyte, B cell), set by developmental history and largely irreversible. A cell state is a reversible condition within a type (naive, activated, exhausted, cycling). Clustering does not know the difference. A cluster of cycling cells will contain CD4 T, CD8 T and NK cells that happen to be in S/G2M; an “activated” cluster may pool several lineages that share an interferon response. Annotation therefore proceeds hierarchically: first lineage, then state within lineage, often by subclustering.


4.1.2 Marker-based annotation
The fastest route to a first-pass annotation is a panel of markers you already trust as an immunologist. The table below is a starting point for human PBMCs.

Markers that betray you. CD4 mRNA is barely detectable in CD4 T cells; you will see more CD4 in monocytes. FOXP3 drops out in most Tregs. CD8A alone does not separate CD8 T from NK or γδ. Always annotate from a set of markers and a pattern across clusters (dot plots), never from one gene in one cell.



4.1.3 Differential expression between clusters
Marker discovery tests each gene for higher expression in one cluster versus all others. The Wilcoxon rank-sum test is the default and is adequate for finding markers. Its p-values, however, are not valid inference:

Double dipping. We defined clusters by finding groups of cells with different expression, then test whether their expression differs. The null hypothesis was falsified by construction. Cluster-marker p-values are useful for ranking genes, not for claiming a population is “significantly” different. For real inferential questions (Does exhaustion differ between responders and non-responders?) you need biological replicates and pseudobulk methods, which we cover in Week 6.

Rank markers by effect size (log fold change, fraction of cells expressing) rather than by p-value, and require that a marker be expressed in a substantial fraction of the cluster (min.pct / pts).


4.1.4 Reference-based annotation
Rather than annotating from scratch, you can transfer labels from a curated reference atlas. Azimuth (Seurat) maps your cells onto a reference PBMC atlas using anchors in a shared low-dimensional space and transfers labels at three levels of granularity, with a per-cell mapping score. CellTypist (Python) is a logistic-regression classifier trained on hundreds of thousands of curated immune cells, with models at several resolutions and a majority-voting step that smooths predictions over your own clusters.
Reference annotation is fast, consistent across studies and excellent at catching things you would miss (a handful of pDCs, a CD4 CTL cluster). It fails on populations absent from the reference (disease-specific states, exhausted cells in a healthy-PBMC reference) and cannot tell you when it is wrong; the mapping score can only flag when it is uncertain. Treat it as a second opinion to reconcile with your manual annotation, not as ground truth.


4.1.5 Subclustering
T cell states that matter to immunologists (naive vs central memory, Treg vs activated CD4, MAIT vs effector CD8) live in a small corner of the total variance and are often merged at the global resolution. Standard practice is to subset the T cells, recompute HVGs and PCA on that subset (so the components now describe variation within T cells rather than T-vs-monocyte), and cluster again.

4.3 Pitfalls


Annotating from one gene. CD4+ by mRNA misses most CD4 T cells and catches monocytes.
Naming every cluster as a distinct subset. Some clusters are the same population at different activation levels, or the same lineage in different cell-cycle phases.
Trusting reference labels blindly. A healthy-PBMC reference will label exhausted tumour T cells as “CD8 TEM”. Check mapping scores and marker expression.
Reporting Wilcoxon p-values as evidence. They rank markers; they do not test hypotheses about populations you defined from the same data.
Skipping re-computation when subclustering. Reusing global PCs on a T cell subset leaves you clustering on T-vs-myeloid noise.
Missing contaminants and doublets. A cluster expressing CD3E and LYZ and MS4A1 is doublets, not a trispecific cell.

title: 5  TCR Repertoire Analysis
text:
5.1.1 V(D)J recombination, briefly
Each αβ T cell expresses one TCR made of a TRA chain (V–J recombination) and a TRB chain (V–D–J recombination). The junctional region, CDR3, contains the V/J (and D) ends plus non-templated nucleotides added by TdT; it is hypervariable and is the main determinant of antigen specificity, so it is what we use to identify a clone. Because the two alleles rearrange independently and allelic exclusion is incomplete for TRA, roughly 10–30% of T cells carry two productive TRA chains (one of which may not pair or be surface-expressed) and ~1% carry two TRB.







 A TRB transcript. Cell Ranger assembles the full contig; we mostly use CDR3 plus V and J gene calls. 





5.1.2 What Cell Ranger gives you
cellranger vdj (or multi) assembles contigs per cell barcode and annotates them. The key file is filtered_contig_annotations.csv, one row per contig (chain), with columns:







Column
Meaning




barcode
Cell barcode; matches GEX barcodes when run through multi on the same lane


chain
TRA, TRB (also TRD, TRG, or Multi for ambiguous)


v_gene, d_gene, j_gene, c_gene
Gene segment calls


cdr3, cdr3_nt
CDR3 amino-acid and nucleotide sequence


productive
In-frame, no stop codon, complete V–J


high_confidence, full_length, is_cell
Assembly quality flags


umis, reads
Support for the contig


raw_clonotype_id
Cell Ranger’s own clonotype (paired nucleotide CDR3)



A typical 5′ run recovers a productive TRB in 70–90% of T cells and a productive TRA in 60–80%; full αβ pairing in 50–70%. Missing chains are dropout, not evidence of a γδ or CD3-negative cell.


5.1.3 Defining a clonotype

There is no single definition of a clonotype. A clonotype is a set of cells you decide to treat as descendants of one naive T cell. Common rules, from strictest to loosest:

Paired CDR3 nucleotide (TRA nt + TRB nt): the closest to true clonal identity. Cells missing a chain cannot be assigned, so ~30% of cells are lost.
Paired CDR3 amino acid: collapses convergent recombinations that produce the same protein. Slightly looser; same dropout problem.
TRB CDR3 nt + V gene (β only): maximises the number of assignable cells; risks merging distinct clones that share a β chain (rare for private clones, common for invariant populations).
TRB CDR3 aa: loosest; will merge public clones with different nucleotide origins.

State your rule in every figure legend. For expansion analysis, use paired-chain definitions and report the fraction of cells that were assignable. For counting clonotypes across samples where dropout differs, consider β-only for consistency.


Invariant and semi-invariant T cells. MAIT cells almost all use TRAV1-2–TRAJ33/12/20 with a CDR3α of canonical length; iNKT cells use TRAV10–TRAJ18. By a TRA-based definition these would appear as a massively “expanded” clone. Always check whether a large clonotype is an invariant population before calling it an expansion. Conversely, your Week 4 MAIT cluster can now be validated: >90% of its cells should carry TRAV1-2.



5.1.4 Quantifying expansion and diversity
Clonal expansion is the observation that a clonotype occupies more than one cell. In healthy blood most clonotypes are singletons; a few (often cytotoxic CD8 TEMRA, or CMV-specific) are large. Convention is to bin clone sizes (1, 2–5, 6–20, 21–100, >100) or to use proportion of repertoire.
Diversity indices summarise the clone-size distribution in one number:








Index
What it emphasises
Sensitive to




Richness (number of unique clonotypes)
How many clones
Sequencing depth and cell number, strongly


Shannon entropy
Both richness and evenness
Cell number, moderately


Simpson / inverse Simpson
Dominance of large clones
Least sensitive to rare clones


Gini coefficient
Inequality of clone sizes (0 = all equal, 1 = one clone)
Good for expansion, independent of richness


Chao1
Estimated true richness including unseen clones
Extrapolation assumptions


D50
Fraction of clonotypes needed to make up 50% of cells
Intuitive; depends on cell number




Diversity depends on how many cells you sequenced. A sample with 5,000 T cells will always show more clonotypes than one with 500. Compare samples only after downsampling to equal cell numbers, or use indices designed to be depth-robust (inverse Simpson, Gini), and report the cell counts.



5.1.5 From sequence to specificity
Clonotype identity is exact; specificity is fuzzy. TCRs that differ by one or two CDR3 residues often recognise the same peptide–MHC. Methods such as TCRdist, GLIPH2 and scirpy’s alignment distance group TCRs into specificity clusters by sequence similarity, letting you ask whether several distinct clones are converging on one antigen. Databases (VDJdb, McPAS-TCR, IEDB) list TCRs with known specificity; you will find matches for common viral epitopes (CMV pp65, EBV BMLF1, influenza M1) in most donors.

library(Seurat)

table(contigs$chain, contigs$productive)

# combineTCR: filters to productive TRA/TRB, keeps up to 2 TRA + 1 TRB per cell,
# and builds per-cell clonotype strings (CTgene, CTnt, CTaa, CTstrict)
combined <- combineTCR(
  list(PBMC = contigs),
  samples = "PBMC",
  removeNA = FALSE,           # keep single-chain cells; drop them later if you wish
  removeMulti = FALSE,        # TRUE drops cells with > 2 chains of one type (likely doublets)
  filterMultimapper = TRUE
)
head(combined$PBMC[, c("barcode", "TCR1", "cdr3_aa1", "TCR2", "cdr3_aa2", "CTstrict")])


import scanpy as sc
import scirpy as ir
import mudata as mu
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

tcells = sc.read_h5ad("data/processed/04_tcells.h5ad")
airr   = ir.io.read_10x_vdj("data/raw/filtered_contig_annotations.csv")

# Build a MuData with paired gex + airr modalities (scirpy >= 0.13 convention)
mdata = mu.MuData({"gex": tcells, "airr": airr})
mdata

# Chain indexing picks the most-supported productive TRA/TRB per cell and
# records secondary chains; chain_qc classifies receptor types
ir.pp.index_chains(mdata)
ir.tl.chain_qc(mdata)

mdata.obs["airr:chain_pairing"].value_counts()
ir.pl.group_abundance(mdata, groupby="airr:receptor_subtype", target_col="gex:celltype")





5.2.2 Define clonotypes and attach to the expression object

R (scRepertoire)Python (scirpy)


# Attach TCR to Seurat. cloneCall options: "gene", "nt", "aa", "strict" (gene+nt)
# Barcodes must match: scRepertoire prefixes with sample name, so strip that
combined$PBMC$barcode <- sub("^PBMC_", "", combined$PBMC$barcode)

tcells <- combineExpression(
  combined, tcells,
  cloneCall  = "strict",
  group.by   = "sample",
  proportion = FALSE,
  cloneSize  = c(Single = 1, Small = 5, Medium = 20, Large = 100, Hyperexpanded = 500)
)

# What fraction of T cells received a TCR?
mean(!is.na(tcells$CTstrict))
table(tcells$cloneSize, useNA = "ifany")

# Validate the MAIT cluster
tcells$is_TRAV1_2 <- grepl("TRAV1-2", tcells$CTgene)
prop.table(table(tcells$seurat_clusters, tcells$is_TRAV1_2), margin = 1)


# Distance between receptors; "identity" = exact match on CDR3 nt
ir.pp.ir_dist(mdata, metric="identity", sequence="nt")

# Clonotype = identical CDR3 nt on both chains plus same V genes (strict);
# receptor_arms="all" requires all present chains to match, dual_ir="primary_only"
ir.tl.define_clonotypes(
    mdata, receptor_arms="all", dual_ir="primary_only",
    same_v_gene=True, key_added="clone_id"
)

ir.tl.clonal_expansion(mdata, target_col="clone_id", key_added="clonal_expansion")
mdata.obs["airr:clonal_expansion"].value_counts()

# Push AIRR-derived columns into the gex modality for plotting
mu.pp.intersect_obs(mdata)   # optional: keep only cells with both modalities
mdata.obs["gex:clone_id"]          = mdata.obs["airr:clone_id"]
mdata.obs["gex:clonal_expansion"]  = mdata.obs["airr:clonal_expansion"]

# Validate MAIT cluster by TRAV1-2 usage
v_alpha = ir.get.airr(mdata, "v_call", chain="VJ_1")
mdata.obs["gex:is_TRAV1_2"] = (v_alpha == "TRAV1-2").values
pd.crosstab(mdata.obs["gex:t_leiden"], mdata.obs["gex:is_TRAV1_2"], normalize="index")





5.2.3 Expansion and diversity

R (scRepertoire)Python (scirpy)


# Repertoire-level summaries operate on the combined list
clonalQuant(combined,     cloneCall = "strict", chain = "both", scale = TRUE)
clonalAbundance(combined, cloneCall = "strict", scale = FALSE)
clonalLength(combined,    cloneCall = "aa", chain = "TRB")
clonalHomeostasis(combined, cloneCall = "strict",
                  cloneSize = c(Rare = 1e-4, Small = 1e-3, Medium = 1e-2, Large = 1e-1, Hyperexpanded = 1))

# Diversity with bootstrapped downsampling to the smallest group
clonalDiversity(combined, cloneCall = "strict", n.boots = 100)

# Per-phenotype diversity: split the Seurat object by cluster
by_cluster <- expression2List(tcells, split.by = "seurat_clusters")
clonalDiversity(by_cluster, cloneCall = "strict", metrics = c("shannon", "inv.simpson", "gini.coeff"))


# Clone-size distribution per T cell cluster
ir.pl.clonal_expansion(mdata, target_col="clone_id", groupby="gex:t_leiden",
                       clip_at=4, normalize=True)

# Diversity per cluster; try metric="normalized_shannon_entropy" or "D50"
ir.pl.alpha_diversity(mdata, groupby="gex:t_leiden", target_col="clone_id",
                      metric="normalized_shannon_entropy")

# Depth-matched comparison: subsample each cluster to the smallest n before scoring
def downsampled_diversity(obs, group_col, clone_col, n=None, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    n = n or obs.groupby(group_col).size().min()
    out = {}
    for g, df in obs.groupby(group_col):
        sub = df.sample(n, random_state=seed) if len(df) > n else df
        counts = sub[clone_col].value_counts()
        p = counts / counts.sum()
        out[g] = -(p * np.log(p)).sum()
    return pd.Series(out, name="shannon")

downsampled_diversity(mdata.obs.dropna(subset=["airr:clone_id"]),
                      "gex:t_leiden", "airr:clone_id")

# Most expanded clonotypes and their gene usage
ir.pl.group_abundance(mdata, groupby="airr:clone_id", target_col="gex:t_leiden", max_cols=15)
ir.pl.vdj_usage(mdata, full_combination=False, max_segments=None, max_ribbons=30)





5.2.4 Clonotype meets phenotype
The central question of paired GEX + TCR data: where do expanded clones live, and do the cells of one clone share a state?

R (scRepertoire)Python (scirpy)


# Clone size on the UMAP
DimPlot(tcells, group.by = "cloneSize", order = TRUE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = rev(colorblind_vector()[c(1,3,4,5,7)]), na.value = "grey90")

# Contour overlay of expanded clones
clonalOverlay(tcells, reduction = "umap", cut.category = "clonalFrequency",
              cutpoint = 5, bins = 10, facet.by = NULL)

# Which clusters are occupied by expanded vs singleton clones?
clonalOccupy(tcells, x.axis = "seurat_clusters", proportion = TRUE)

# Do sister cells of one clone share a cluster? Highlight the top 5 clones.
top_clones <- names(sort(table(tcells$CTstrict), decreasing = TRUE))[1:5]
tcells <- highlightClones(tcells, cloneCall = "strict", sequence = top_clones)
DimPlot(tcells, group.by = "highlight", order = TRUE) + NoLegend()

# Clone-sharing between clusters (a clone whose cells span two clusters connects them)
clonalNetwork(tcells, reduction = "umap", group.by = "seurat_clusters",
              filter.clones = NULL, filter.identity = NULL, cloneCall = "strict")

# STARTRAC-style: transitional index measures clones spanning multiple states
StartracDiversity(tcells, type = "seurat_clusters", group.by = "sample")

saveRDS(tcells, "data/processed/05_tcells_tcr.rds")


# Clone size on the UMAP
sc.pl.umap(mdata["gex"], color="clonal_expansion", frameon=False)

# Occupancy: clone-size composition of each cluster
ir.pl.clonal_expansion(mdata, target_col="clone_id", groupby="gex:t_leiden", normalize=True)

# Highlight the five largest clonotypes
top = mdata.obs["airr:clone_id"].value_counts().head(5).index
mdata.obs["gex:top_clone"] = mdata.obs["airr:clone_id"].where(
    mdata.obs["airr:clone_id"].isin(top), other=np.nan)
sc.pl.umap(mdata["gex"], color="top_clone", frameon=False, na_color="lightgrey")

# Cluster distribution of each top clone: do sister cells share a state?
pd.crosstab(mdata.obs["airr:clone_id"], mdata.obs["gex:t_leiden"]).loc[top]

# Clonotype network: nodes = clonotypes, size = cells, colour = dominant cluster
ir.tl.clonotype_network(mdata, min_cells=2, clonotype_key="clone_id")
ir.pl.clonotype_network(mdata, color="gex:t_leiden", panel_size=(7, 7), base_size=10)

mdata.write("data/processed/05_tcells_tcr.h5mu")

title: 5  TCR Repertoire Analysis
text:
5.3 Pitfalls


Not stating the clonotype definition. Numbers of clonotypes and expansion levels change substantially between nt-paired and aa-β-only rules.
Comparing diversity across samples of different size. Always downsample or use depth-robust indices.
Calling MAIT / iNKT an expanded clone. Check TRAV1-2 / TRAV10 before interpreting a large “clone”.
Treating cells with two TRB as dual-TCR cells. Most are doublets; cross-check with your doublet scores.
Treating missing chains as biology. A TRB-only cell is a dropout, not a pre-selection thymocyte.
Over-reading database hits. A CDR3β match to a CMV epitope in VDJdb suggests, not proves, CMV specificity; α chain and HLA context matter.
Ignoring barcode conventions. Cell Ranger suffixes (-1), scRepertoire prefixes and multi-lane merging all change barcode strings. Check the overlap between GEX and TCR barcodes before attaching.

title: 6  Multi-sample Analysis and Capstone
text: 6.1 Concepts

title: 6  Multi-sample Analysis and Capstone
text:
6.1.1 Batch effects
Cells processed on different days, by different hands, in different 10x lanes, or from different donors differ systematically in ways unrelated to the biology you care about. In a UMAP, the same cell type from two batches forms two islands. Left uncorrected, batch will dominate clustering and every “condition-specific cluster” will be a batch-specific cluster.

Batch is confounded with biology by design in most experiments. Patients versus controls, pre- versus post-treatment, tumour versus blood: these usually arrive in different batches. No algorithm can separate a batch effect from a biological effect when they are perfectly confounded. Integration methods assume that the same cell types exist in every batch and align them. If a cell state truly exists only in one condition, aggressive integration will erase it. The defences are experimental (process conditions together, multiplex with hashing or genotype) and analytical (integrate conservatively, check that condition-specific populations survive, and never test DE on integrated values).



6.1.2 Integration methods
All integration methods find a shared representation in which cells of the same type from different batches overlap. They differ in what they modify:

Harmony operates on the PCA embedding. It iteratively clusters cells, computes per-batch cluster centroids, and shifts each cell’s PC coordinates to remove batch-specific offsets. Fast, works on large data, and leaves expression values untouched. The corrected embedding is used for the kNN graph, clustering and UMAP.
Seurat anchors (CCA / RPCA) find pairs of mutually similar cells across batches (“anchors”), then use them to learn a correction. CCA is more aggressive (good when batches are very different, risks over-correction); RPCA is more conservative (good when you expect real condition differences). Seurat v5’s IntegrateLayers returns a corrected embedding.
scVI / scANVI fit a deep generative model of counts with batch as a covariate; the latent space is batch-corrected and can also denoise expression. Best for very large or highly heterogeneous datasets, at the cost of GPU time and more hyperparameters.

Whichever you choose, assess it: cell types should mix across batches (a low batch-LISI or high batch mixing score) while remaining separated from each other (high cell-type silhouette). Over-correction looks like everything merged into a blob.


6.1.3 Differential expression between conditions: pseudobulk
The question “Is GZMB higher in effector CD8 T cells from patients than from controls?” has a sample size equal to the number of patients, not the number of cells. Ten thousand cells from three patients are three biological replicates with a great deal of within-replicate measurement.

Pseudoreplication. Treating cells as independent observations inflates the sample size by orders of magnitude and produces astronomically small p-values for tiny effects, including effects driven by a single unusual donor. Every single-cell DE method that tests cell-vs-cell across conditions (Wilcoxon, MAST, single-cell t-tests) has this problem.
Pseudobulk fixes it by summing counts across all cells of a given type within each sample, producing one expression profile per sample per cell type. You then run bulk RNA-seq DE methods (edgeR, DESeq2, limma) with samples as the unit of replication. Benchmarks consistently show pseudobulk methods have the best false-discovery control. The requirement: at least 3, preferably more, biological replicates per condition.



6.1.4 Compositional changes
“Are there more Tregs in patients?” is a question about proportions. Cell-type proportions within a sample are not independent (if Tregs go up, something else goes down), and they vary hugely between donors. Test at the sample level: compute per-sample proportions and use a method that handles compositional data and replicate variability (propeller in R, scCODA in Python). Do not run a chi-squared test on pooled cell counts; that suffers from pseudoreplication too.


6.1.5 Tracking clonotypes across samples
With TCR data from multiple samples of the same individual (blood and tumour, pre- and post-treatment, multiple timepoints), a clonotype becomes a lineage barcode you can follow. Questions become answerable: Did the clones that expanded after treatment exist before it? Do tumour-infiltrating clones also circulate? Did an exhausted clone’s sister cells in blood look naive or effector? Because each individual has a unique repertoire, clonotype tracking is always within-donor; overlap between donors is limited to public clones and is itself a finding.

title: 6  Multi-sample Analysis and Capstone
text:
6.2 Hands-on
For this chapter you need at least two samples. If you have only the single donor dataset, split it artificially by lane or randomly to practise the mechanics, but remember the biology will be null. The Setup appendix lists suitable public multi-sample datasets.

6.2.1 Merge and inspect before integrating

R (Seurat)Python (Scanpy)


library(Seurat)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# Assume a list of per-sample Seurat objects, each already QC'd (Week 1)
objs <- list(
  ctrl1 = readRDS("data/processed/ctrl1_qc.rds"),
  ctrl2 = readRDS("data/processed/ctrl2_qc.rds"),
  pat1  = readRDS("data/processed/pat1_qc.rds"),
  pat2  = readRDS("data/processed/pat2_qc.rds")
)
for (n in names(objs)) { objs[[n]]$sample <- n; objs[[n]]$condition <- sub("\\d$", "", n) }

# Seurat v5 keeps samples as layers within one assay
merged <- merge(objs[[1]], objs[-1], add.cell.ids = names(objs))
merged <- NormalizeData(merged) %>% FindVariableFeatures() %>% ScaleData() %>%
  RunPCA(verbose = FALSE)
merged <- FindNeighbors(merged, dims = 1:30) %>% FindClusters(resolution = 0.5) %>%
  RunUMAP(dims = 1:30, reduction.name = "umap.unintegrated")

# How bad is the batch effect? Same cell types should overlap across samples
DimPlot(merged, reduction = "umap.unintegrated", group.by = c("sample", "seurat_clusters"))


import scanpy as sc
import anndata as ad
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

samples = ["ctrl1", "ctrl2", "pat1", "pat2"]
adatas = {s: sc.read_h5ad(f"data/processed/{s}_qc.h5ad") for s in samples}
adata = ad.concat(adatas, label="sample", index_unique="-")
adata.obs["condition"] = adata.obs["sample"].str.replace(r"\d$", "", regex=True)
adata.layers["counts"] = adata.X.copy()

sc.pp.normalize_total(adata, target_sum=1e4); sc.pp.log1p(adata)
sc.pp.highly_variable_genes(adata, n_top_genes=2000, flavor="seurat_v3",
                            layer="counts", batch_key="sample")
adata.raw = adata
sc.pp.scale(adata, max_value=10)
sc.tl.pca(adata, n_comps=50, mask_var="highly_variable")
sc.pp.neighbors(adata, n_pcs=30); sc.tl.leiden(adata, resolution=0.5, flavor="igraph", n_iterations=2)
sc.tl.umap(adata)
adata.obsm["X_umap_unintegrated"] = adata.obsm["X_umap"].copy()
sc.pl.umap(adata, color=["sample", "leiden"], frameon=False)





6.2.2 Integrate

R (Seurat)Python (Scanpy)


# Harmony (fast, embedding-level). Requires the 'harmony' package.
merged <- IntegrateLayers(merged, method = HarmonyIntegration,
                          orig.reduction = "pca", new.reduction = "harmony",
                          verbose = FALSE)

# Alternative: RPCA anchors, more conservative
# merged <- IntegrateLayers(merged, method = RPCAIntegration,
#                           orig.reduction = "pca", new.reduction = "integrated.rpca")

merged <- FindNeighbors(merged, reduction = "harmony", dims = 1:30) %>%
  FindClusters(resolution = 0.5, cluster.name = "harmony_clusters") %>%
  RunUMAP(reduction = "harmony", dims = 1:30, reduction.name = "umap.harmony")

DimPlot(merged, reduction = "umap.harmony", group.by = c("sample", "harmony_clusters"))
DimPlot(merged, reduction = "umap.harmony", split.by = "condition", group.by = "harmony_clusters")

# Rejoin layers before DE / marker finding
merged <- JoinLayers(merged)


# Harmony via harmonypy
sc.external.pp.harmony_integrate(adata, key="sample", basis="X_pca",
                                 adjusted_basis="X_pca_harmony")
sc.pp.neighbors(adata, use_rep="X_pca_harmony", n_pcs=30)
sc.tl.leiden(adata, resolution=0.5, key_added="harmony_leiden", flavor="igraph", n_iterations=2)
sc.tl.umap(adata)
sc.pl.umap(adata, color=["sample", "harmony_leiden"], frameon=False)
sc.pl.umap(adata, color="harmony_leiden", groups=None, frameon=False)

# Alternative: scVI (GPU recommended)
# import scvi
# scvi.model.SCVI.setup_anndata(adata, layer="counts", batch_key="sample")
# model = scvi.model.SCVI(adata); model.train()
# adata.obsm["X_scVI"] = model.get_latent_representation()

# Assess mixing: cells of one type should draw neighbours from all samples
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors
nn = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=30).fit(adata.obsm["X_pca_harmony"][:, :30])
idx = nn.kneighbors(return_distance=False)
same_sample = (adata.obs["sample"].values[idx] == adata.obs["sample"].values[:, None]).mean(1)
adata.obs["frac_same_sample_nn"] = same_sample
print("Expected if perfectly mixed:", (adata.obs['sample'].value_counts(normalize=True)**2).sum())
print("Observed mean:", same_sample.mean())





6.2.3 Annotate the integrated object
Reuse Week 4: marker dot plot plus reference labels, then assign celltype. Check specifically whether any cluster is composed of cells from one condition only; that is either the finding of the study or an under-corrected batch, and you must decide which from markers and from replicate consistency (does it appear in both patients?).


6.2.4 Pseudobulk differential expression

R (Seurat + edgeR)Python (decoupler + PyDESeq2)


library(edgeR)

# Sum raw counts per sample x cell type
pb <- AggregateExpression(merged, assays = "RNA", slot = "counts",
                          group.by = c("celltype", "sample"), return.seurat = FALSE)$RNA
colnames(pb)   # e.g. "CD8 T effector_ctrl1"

# Test one cell type: effector CD8 T, patients vs controls
ct   <- "CD8 T effector"
keep <- grepl(paste0("^", ct, "_"), colnames(pb))
y    <- DGEList(counts = pb[, keep])
y$samples$sample    <- sub(".*_", "", colnames(y))
y$samples$condition <- factor(sub("\\d$", "", y$samples$sample), levels = c("ctrl", "pat"))

# Require enough cells per pseudobulk to be meaningful
ncells <- table(merged$celltype, merged$sample)[ct, y$samples$sample]
stopifnot(all(ncells >= 20))

y <- y[filterByExpr(y, group = y$samples$condition), , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE]
y <- calcNormFactors(y)
design <- model.matrix(~ condition, data = y$samples)
y   <- estimateDisp(y, design)
fit <- glmQLFit(y, design)
res <- glmQLFTest(fit, coef = "conditionpat")
topTags(res, n = 20)

# Compare with the WRONG approach to see the inflation
wrong <- FindMarkers(subset(merged, celltype == ct), ident.1 = "pat", ident.2 = "ctrl",
                     group.by = "condition", test.use = "wilcox")
c(pseudobulk_sig = sum(topTags(res, n = Inf)$table$FDR < 0.05),
  wilcoxon_sig   = sum(wrong$p_val_adj < 0.05))


# pip install decoupler pydeseq2
import decoupler as dc
from pydeseq2.dds import DeseqDataSet
from pydeseq2.ds import DeseqStats

pdata = dc.pp.pseudobulk(
    adata, sample_col="sample", groups_col="celltype",
    layer="counts", mode="sum", min_cells=20, min_counts=1000
)
pdata.obs["condition"] = pdata.obs["sample"].str.replace(r"\d$", "", regex=True)

ct  = "CD8 T effector"
sub = pdata[pdata.obs["celltype"] == ct].copy()
dc.pp.filter_by_expr(sub, group="condition", min_count=10, min_total_count=15)

dds = DeseqDataSet(adata=sub, design="~condition", refit_cooks=True, quiet=True)
dds.deseq2()
stat = DeseqStats(dds, contrast=["condition", "pat", "ctrl"], quiet=True)
stat.summary()
res = stat.results_df.sort_values("padj")
res.head(20)

# The WRONG way, for comparison
cells = adata[adata.obs["celltype"] == ct].copy()
sc.tl.rank_genes_groups(cells, "condition", groups=["pat"], reference="ctrl",
                        method="wilcoxon", use_raw=True)
wrong = sc.get.rank_genes_groups_df(cells, "pat")
print("pseudobulk sig:", (res["padj"] < 0.05).sum(),
      "| wilcoxon sig:", (wrong["pvals_adj"] < 0.05).sum())

# BiocManager::install("speckle")
library(speckle)
props <- propeller(clusters = merged$celltype, sample = merged$sample,
                   group = merged$condition, transform = "logit")
props

plotCellTypeProps(clusters = merged$celltype, sample = merged$sample) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))


# pip install pertpy   (scCODA is bundled)
import pertpy as pt

sccoda = pt.tl.Sccoda()
cdata  = sccoda.load(adata, type="cell_level", generate_sample_level=True,
                     cell_type_identifier="celltype", sample_identifier="sample",
                     covariate_obs=["condition"])
cdata  = sccoda.prepare(cdata, formula="condition", reference_cell_type="automatic")
sccoda.run_nuts(cdata, rng_key=0)
sccoda.summary(cdata)
sccoda.credible_effects(cdata)

# Simple per-sample proportion plot
prop = pd.crosstab(adata.obs["sample"], adata.obs["celltype"], normalize="index")
prop.plot.bar(stacked=True, figsize=(6, 4), colormap="tab20").legend(bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1))





6.2.6 Track clonotypes across samples

R (scRepertoire)Python (scirpy)


library(scRepertoire)
contig_list <- list(
  ctrl1 = read.csv("data/raw/ctrl1/filtered_contig_annotations.csv"),
  pat1_blood  = read.csv("data/raw/pat1_blood/filtered_contig_annotations.csv"),
  pat1_tumour = read.csv("data/raw/pat1_tumour/filtered_contig_annotations.csv")
)
combined <- combineTCR(contig_list, samples = names(contig_list))

# Overlap between samples (within-patient overlap is the interesting one)
clonalOverlap(combined, cloneCall = "strict", method = "morisita")

# Alluvial tracking of the top clones between blood and tumour
clonalCompare(combined, top.clones = 10, samples = c("pat1_blood", "pat1_tumour"),
              cloneCall = "aa", graph = "alluvial")

# Scatter: clone frequency in blood vs tumour
clonalScatter(combined, cloneCall = "strict", x.axis = "pat1_blood", y.axis = "pat1_tumour",
              graph = "proportion")

# Attach to the integrated object and ask which phenotype tumour-expanded clones
# have in blood
merged <- combineExpression(combined, merged, cloneCall = "strict", group.by = "sample")
shared <- intersect(combined$pat1_blood$CTstrict, combined$pat1_tumour$CTstrict)
merged$in_tumour_and_blood <- merged$CTstrict %in% shared
table(merged$celltype[merged$in_tumour_and_blood & merged$sample == "pat1_blood"])


import scirpy as ir, mudata as mu
airr = ir.io.read_10x_vdj  # for each sample, read + concat with matching obs index
# ... assume mdata built as in Week 5, with obs "sample" and "clone_id" over all samples

# Repertoire overlap between samples
df, dist, link = ir.tl.repertoire_overlap(mdata, groupby="sample", target_col="clone_id",
                                          inplace=False)
ir.pl.repertoire_overlap(mdata, groupby="sample", heatmap_cats=["condition"])

# Which clonotypes are shared between blood and tumour of the same patient?
ct = pd.crosstab(mdata.obs["airr:clone_id"], mdata.obs["gex:sample"])
shared = ct.index[(ct["pat1_blood"] > 0) & (ct["pat1_tumour"] > 0)]
print(len(shared), "clonotypes shared between blood and tumour")

# Phenotype of shared clones in blood versus tumour
sub = mdata.obs[mdata.obs["airr:clone_id"].isin(shared)]
pd.crosstab(sub["gex:sample"], sub["gex:celltype"], normalize="index").round(2)

# Clonotype network coloured by sample: nodes spanning samples are shared clones
ir.tl.clonotype_network(mdata, min_cells=2, clonotype_key="clone_id")
ir.pl.clonotype_network(mdata, color="gex:sample", panel_size=(7, 7))

title: 6  Multi-sample Analysis and Capstone
text:
6.3 Pitfalls


Testing DE on integrated or scaled values. Integration corrects an embedding, not the biology. Always go back to raw counts for pseudobulk.
Cells as replicates. Three patients are three replicates, whatever the cell count. If you have n = 1 per condition, you can describe but not test.
Integrating away the finding. A population present only in disease may be erased by CCA. Try a conservative method and confirm the population is absent in every control.
Confounded design. If all patients were processed on Monday and all controls on Tuesday, no method can rescue the comparison. Say so in the paper.
Composition tests on pooled counts. Chi-squared on the total cell table ignores donor variability.
Cross-donor clonotype overlap as “shared response”. Different donors have different repertoires; overlap is mostly public/invariant clones.

title: 6  Multi-sample Analysis and Capstone
text:
6.4 Capstone project
Choose a public multi-sample dataset with paired GEX and TCR (suggestions in the Setup appendix) or use your own. Produce a reproducible report (Quarto, Rmarkdown or Jupyter) that:

QC — states thresholds, cell counts before/after, doublet rates per lane
Processing — normalization method, HVG count with V(D)J exclusion, number of PCs with justification, integration method and an assessment of mixing
Annotation — clusters at a stated resolution, a marker dot plot, agreement with a reference, and a cell-type UMAP; T cells subclustered
Repertoire — clonotype definition stated, fraction of T cells assigned, expansion by cluster, depth-matched diversity, at least one clone-phenotype result
Comparison — one pseudobulk DE result and one compositional result across condition, each with the number of biological replicates stated; one clonotype-tracking result if samples are paired
One figure you would put in a paper, with a legend that would let a reader reproduce it
A limitations paragraph: confounding, replicate number, and which of your conclusions is a hypothesis versus a supported claim

Presentations are 10 minutes plus 5 for questions. You will be assessed on the defensibility of your choices, not on the novelty of your findings.

title: Glossary
text:
Ambient RNA

Cell-free mRNA in the cell suspension, released by lysed cells, that is captured in every droplet. Produces low-level “expression” of highly abundant genes (haemoglobin, TCR constant genes, LYZ) in cells that do not express them.

Anchors

In Seurat integration, pairs of cells from different batches identified as mutual nearest neighbours in a shared space. Used to learn a batch correction.

AnnData

Python container for single-cell data (obs = cell metadata, var = gene metadata, X = expression matrix, obsm = per-cell matrices like PCA/UMAP). The Scanpy equivalent of a Seurat object.

Batch effect

Systematic technical variation between groups of samples processed separately (day, operator, lane, reagent lot) that is unrelated to the biological question.

Cell barcode

A ~16-nt sequence shared by every molecule captured in one droplet. Identifies the (putative) cell.

CDR3

Complementarity-determining region 3; the hypervariable V–(D)–J junction of a TCR or BCR chain. The primary determinant of antigen specificity and the sequence used to define clonotypes.

Clonotype

A set of cells inferred to descend from one naive T cell, defined by an explicit rule on TCR sequence (e.g. identical paired CDR3 nucleotide sequences). The definition is a choice; state it.

Clonal expansion

A clonotype represented by more than one cell, indicating proliferation after antigen encounter.

Community detection

Graph algorithms (Louvain, Leiden) that partition nodes into densely connected groups by maximising modularity. What “clustering” means in single-cell analysis.

Doublet

A droplet containing two cells. Heterotypic (different types) doublets form spurious intermediate clusters; homotypic doublets are hard to detect but appear as dual-TCR cells.

Elbow plot

Variance explained per principal component, in order. Used to choose how many PCs to retain.

Embedding

The coordinates of cells in a reduced space (PCA, Harmony-corrected PCA, UMAP).

Feature

A gene (or protein, in CITE-seq). Seurat’s word for a row of the count matrix.

Highly variable genes (HVGs)

Genes whose variance across cells exceeds the expectation from their mean; used as input to PCA.

Integration

Aligning cells of the same type across batches in a shared embedding so that clustering reflects biology rather than batch.

k-nearest neighbours (kNN)

For each cell, the \(k\) cells closest to it in the embedding. The kNN graph is the basis of clustering and UMAP.

Leiden / Louvain

Community detection algorithms. Leiden is the refined, faster successor that guarantees connected communities.

Library size

Total UMIs (or reads) in a cell. Varies for technical reasons; removed by normalization.

Loadings

The weight of each gene on a principal component. Reading loadings tells you what biology (or artefact) a PC captures.

Log-normalization

Scaling each cell to a fixed total (e.g. 10,000) then applying \(\log(x+1)\).

Marker gene

A gene expressed in one population and not (or much less) in others, used for annotation.

Modularity

A score for a graph partition: edges within communities minus the number expected by chance. Louvain/Leiden maximise it.

MuData

Python container for multimodal data; in this course, a GEX AnnData and an AIRR (TCR) AnnData sharing cell indices.

Normalization

Any transformation that makes expression values comparable across cells by removing technical scaling factors.

Pearson residuals

Normalized values from SCTransform-style models: how far an observed count deviates from what a depth-aware negative-binomial model predicts.

Principal component analysis (PCA)

A linear method that finds orthogonal directions of maximum variance in the data. Reduces thousands of correlated genes to tens of informative axes.

Productive

A rearranged TCR chain that is in-frame with no stop codon, capable of producing protein.

Pseudobulk

Summed counts across all cells of one type within one sample, yielding one profile per sample per type. Enables valid differential expression with samples as replicates.

Pseudoreplication

Treating cells as independent replicates when the biological unit of replication is the donor. Inflates significance.

Public clonotype

A TCR sequence found in multiple individuals, usually because it has few N-additions and is easy to generate, or because it targets a common epitope.

Resolution

The Leiden/Louvain parameter that controls community granularity. Higher = more, smaller clusters.

Scaling

Z-scoring each gene across cells (mean 0, SD 1) before PCA so no gene dominates by magnitude.

SCTransform

Regularised negative-binomial normalization producing Pearson residuals.

Shared nearest neighbours (SNN)

A refinement of the kNN graph weighting edges by the Jaccard overlap of two cells’ neighbour sets.

Silhouette

A per-cell score comparing distance to own cluster vs nearest other cluster. Negative values indicate misassignment or ambiguity.

Sparse matrix

A storage format that records only non-zero entries. Essential because >90% of a count matrix is zero.

Specificity cluster

A group of distinct clonotypes with similar CDR3s inferred to recognise the same antigen (TCRdist, GLIPH2).

UMAP

Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection; a non-linear method that lays out the kNN graph in two dimensions, preserving local neighbourhoods. Distances between islands and island sizes are not interpretable.

UMI

Unique molecular identifier; a random ~12-nt tag on each captured mRNA molecule, allowing PCR duplicates to be collapsed so counts reflect molecules, not reads.

V(D)J recombination

Somatic rearrangement of variable, diversity and joining gene segments to generate TCR and BCR diversity.

title: Further Reading
text:
Single-cell best practices (Heumos, Schaar, Lance et al., Nature Reviews Genetics, 2023; online book at https://www.sc-best-practices.org). The most complete current treatment, Python-centred but conceptually language-neutral. Chapters on quality control, normalization, integration, differential expression and clonotype analysis align directly with this course.
Orchestrating Single-Cell Analysis with Bioconductor (https://bioconductor.org/books/OSCA/). The R/Bioconductor equivalent; excellent on the statistics of QC, normalization and feature selection.
Luecken & Theis, “Current best practices in single-cell RNA-seq analysis: a tutorial”, Molecular Systems Biology, 2019. Shorter and slightly dated but still the best single-paper overview.
